claims.text: The target specimen is bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
HfNbTaTiZr can be produced by additive manufacturing.
A practical HfNbTaTiZr specimen exhibits high-entropy-alloy microstructural complexity and defect distributions.
The proposed hybrid model incorporates measured oxygen content, defect densities, and microstructural descriptors.
Archival conductivity data exist for real HfNbTaTiZr specimens containing 1 wt.% oxygen over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Grain size, lattice distortion, and oxygen site occupancy are relevant model inputs for conductivity prediction.
Inert or high-vacuum conditions are typical testing and operational environments for refractory high-entropy alloys.
The oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr matrix is bcc-based.
Approximately 1 wt.% interstitial oxygen and associated point defects significantly alter electron and phonon scattering and conduction pathways in HfNbTaTiZr.
Including experimentally derived defect concentrations and local chemical disorder allows the hybrid model to capture oxygen-related scattering and transport effects.
Idealized analytical models neglect the conductivity effects of oxygen doping and real microstructural heterogeneity.
Conventional perfect-crystal analytical models typically overestimate the conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
The hybrid model will outperform existing analytical perfect-crystal models for thermal and electrical conductivity.
The hybrid model will reduce conductivity prediction error by at least 5%–10% throughout both 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The model's stated applicability is limited to HfNbTaTiZr with up to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen and temperatures no higher than 1200 K.
Model accuracy depends on training-data completeness and fidelity and on assumptions about oxygen distribution and defect evolution.
A never-before-tested 1 wt.% oxygen HfNbTaTiZr specimen will serve as a held-out conductivity benchmark.
Deviation of more than approximately 5% from measured conductivity across the tested range is specified as the falsifying result.
